---
title: "Alpha diversity"
format: html
editor: visual
---

Alpha diversity describes the diversity within a single sample. It can be summarized by several measures, such as richness (the number of OTUs), Shannon diversity or Simpson diversity. These measures differ in how much weight they give to rare OTUs compared to abundant ones, and therefore capture different aspects of the community.

This section documents how to check whether sequencing depth is sufficient to capture the diversity of the samples using rarefaction and extrapolation curves, how to calculate several alpha diversity measures, and how to compare them between sites. To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script `010_alpha_diversity.R` and the example data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

library(phyloseq)
library(iNEXT)
library(ggplot2)
library(multcompView)
library(dplyr)
load("../RData/16S/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
```

For reproducibility, set seeds (random number generation) at the start of this script to always obtain the same results with rarefaction.

```{r}

```

## Rarefaction

Alpha diversity measures, and richness in particular, depend strongly on sequencing depth: the more reads a sample has, the more OTUs are detected. For this reason, rarefaction is recommended before comparing alpha diversity between samples [@schloss2024], even when other standardization methods are used for beta diversity (see [Rarefaction & Normalization](../otu-tables/rare-norm.qmd)).

```{r}
# What is the smallest library size across samples?
min(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)) # 24663 reads

# Rarefy to the library size of the sample with the lowest library size (default)
otu_table_rarefy <- rarefy_even_depth(otu_BLAST_clean, replace = F)

# Check the number of reads per sample: all samples should have the same depth
head(sample_sums(otu_table_rarefy))

# Save the rarefaction depth to use it in the plots below
rare_depth <- min(sample_sums(otu_table_rarefy))

# How many OTUs remained after rarefaction?
ntaxa(otu_BLAST_clean)
ntaxa(otu_table_rarefy)
```

OTUs that only had a few reads in the samples with large library sizes can be lost during rarefaction. `rarefy_even_depth()` removes them automatically from the `phyloseq` object.

## Rarefaction and extrapolation

Rarefaction discards reads. To check whether the rarefaction depth is sufficient to capture the diversity of the samples, we can draw rarefaction and extrapolation curves with the R package `iNEXT` [@chao2014; @hsieh2016]. These curves show how diversity increases with the number of reads, and estimate how it would continue to increase with more reads (extrapolation).

::: callout-note
## Hill numbers

`iNEXT` uses Hill numbers of order *q* [@hill1973; @jost2006]:

-   *q* = 0: species richness (number of OTUs)
-   *q* = 1: Shannon diversity (the exponential of the Shannon entropy)
-   *q* = 2: Simpson diversity (the inverse of the Simpson concentration)

Larger numbers always mean higher diversity. Hill numbers are expressed in "effective number of OTUs": the number of equally abundant OTUs that would give the same diversity. As *q* increases, rare OTUs get less weight. Expressing all three measures in the same unit makes them directly comparable.
:::

`iNEXT` expects a data frame with OTUs as rows and samples as columns. Use the non-rarefied count data, as `iNEXT` performs its own rarefaction.

```{r}
# Convert the OTU table to a data frame with OTUs as rows
otu_df <- as.data.frame(as(otu_table(otu_BLAST_clean), "matrix"))
if (!taxa_are_rows(otu_BLAST_clean)) otu_df <- as.data.frame(t(otu_df))
```

`iNEXT()` is run on each sample individually. Two arguments control the shape and computation time of the curves:

-   `endpoint`: the largest number of reads to extrapolate to. Extrapolation is only reliable up to about twice the library size of the sample [@chao2014].
-   `knots`: the number of points calculated along each curve. Fewer knots make the calculation faster.

```{r}
#| cache: true
# Run iNEXT for each sample individually (it takes a while to run...)
inext_res <- iNEXT(otu_df, q = c(0, 1, 2), datatype = "abundance",
                   endpoint = 2 * rare_depth, knots = 20)
```

### Sample-size-based curves

The rarefaction (solid lines) and extrapolation (dashed lines) curves are plotted for each order *q*. The vertical line shows the rarefaction depth.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggiNEXT(inext_res, type = 1, facet.var = "Order.q", grey = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rare_depth) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

For Shannon and Simpson diversity (*q* = 1 and *q* = 2), the curves reach an asymptote (plateau) well before the rarefaction depth: the rarefied data capture the diversity of the samples. For richness (*q* = 0), the curves keep increasing, which means that more OTUs would be found with more sequencing. Richness is very sensitive to rare OTUs and to sequencing depth, and is therefore the measure that requires the most caution.

### Sample completeness curves

The sample completeness (sample coverage) gives the proportion of the community represented by the OTUs detected in each sample. A coverage close to 1 means that very few new OTUs would be found with more sequencing.

```{r}
#| warning: false
ggiNEXT(inext_res, type = 2, grey = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rare_depth) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Estimated diversity

`iNEXT` also returns the observed and estimated (asymptotic) diversity of each sample. The estimated richness corresponds to the Chao1 estimator [@chao1984], which uses the number of rare OTUs (singletons and doubletons) to estimate how many OTUs remain undetected.

```{r}
inext_div <- inext_res$AsyEst
head(inext_div)
```

## Alpha diversity measures

Alpha diversity can be represented by multiple measures, e.g., richness, Shannon, Simpson, Chao1, etc. Here, we calculate them on the rarefied data using `phyloseq::estimate_richness()`, which calculates several measures at once:

-   `Observed`: the number of OTUs (richness)
-   `Shannon`: the Shannon entropy (H')
-   `InvSimpson`: the inverse Simpson index (= Hill number *q* = 2)

```{r}
alpha_div <- estimate_richness(otu_table_rarefy,
                               measures = c("Observed", "Shannon", "InvSimpson"))
```

The Shannon entropy is then converted to Shannon diversity (= Hill number *q* = 1), so that the three measures are expressed in the same unit (number of OTUs). We also add the estimated richness (Chao1) calculated by `iNEXT` on the non-rarefied data.

```{r}
# Convert the Shannon entropy to Shannon diversity
alpha_div$Shannon_div <- exp(alpha_div$Shannon)

# Add the estimated richness (Chao1) from iNEXT
rich_est <- inext_div %>%
  filter(Diversity == "Species richness") %>%
  select(Assemblage, Estimator) %>%
  dplyr::rename(Chao1 = Estimator)

alpha_div$Chao1 <- rich_est$Chao1[match(rownames(alpha_div), rich_est$Assemblage)]
```

Finally, combine the alpha diversity measures with the sample data. Note that `estimate_richness()` returns the samples in the same order as the `phyloseq` object.

```{r}
# Combine with the sample data
alpha_div <- cbind.data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_rarefy)) %>%
  cbind(alpha_div)

# Look at the data
head(alpha_div[, c("SiteID", "Land_use", "Observed", "Chao1",
                   "Shannon_div", "InvSimpson")])
```

The different measures are often correlated with each other.

```{r}
pairs(alpha_div[, c("Observed", "Chao1", "Shannon_div", "InvSimpson")])
```

## Compare alpha diversity between sites

We now test if alpha diversity differs between sites using an analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by a Tukey test to find which sites differ from each other. The significance letters from the Tukey test (compact letter display) are added to the plots: sites that share a letter are not significantly different.

::: callout-warning
## Pseudoreplication

Each site has 9 samples. The land use types are not replicated in the same way (6 oak forests, but only 1 site for each of the other land uses). Therefore, the samples of one site cannot be used as replicates of a land use, as this would be pseudoreplication [@hurlbert1984]. This is why we compare sites here, and colour the plots by land use.
:::

```{r}
# Order the sites by land use for the plots
alpha_div$SiteID <- factor(alpha_div$SiteID,
                           levels = unique(alpha_div$SiteID[order(alpha_div$Land_use)]))
```

### Richness

First, fit the ANOVA model.

```{r}
M_rich <- aov(Observed ~ SiteID, data = alpha_div)
anova(M_rich)
```

Then, check the assumptions of the ANOVA: the residuals should be normally distributed (Shapiro-Wilk test) and the variances equal between groups (Bartlett test). If not, consider a non-parametric test such as the Kruskal-Wallis test (`kruskal.test()`).

```{r}
shapiro.test(residuals(M_rich))
bartlett.test(Observed ~ SiteID, data = alpha_div)
```

Use a Tukey test to find which sites differ from each other, and summarize the results with a compact letter display.

```{r}
# Tukey test
M_rich_tukey <- TukeyHSD(M_rich)

# Compact letter display
cld_rich <- multcompLetters4(M_rich, M_rich_tukey)

# Table with the mean per site and the significance letters
dt_rich <- group_by(alpha_div, SiteID, Land_use) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(Observed), sd = sd(Observed), .groups = "drop")
dt_rich$cld <- cld_rich$SiteID$Letters[as.character(dt_rich$SiteID)]
```

Finally, plot the mean richness per site, with the significance letters on top of the bars.

```{r}
ggplot(alpha_div, aes(x = SiteID, y = Observed)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = "mean", aes(fill = Land_use)) +
  geom_errorbar(data = dt_rich, aes(y = mean, ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd),
                width = 0.2) +
  geom_jitter(size = 2, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.1) +
  geom_text(data = dt_rich, aes(label = cld, y = max(alpha_div$Observed) * 1.08)) +
  ylab("Bacterial richness (number of OTUs)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

### Estimated richness (Chao1)

We saw that the richness curves did not reach an asymptote. Let's see if the estimated richness shows the same pattern as the observed richness. The same steps are repeated for each measure.

```{r}
# ANOVA
M_chao <- aov(Chao1 ~ SiteID, data = alpha_div)
anova(M_chao)

# Check the assumptions
shapiro.test(residuals(M_chao))
bartlett.test(Chao1 ~ SiteID, data = alpha_div)

# Tukey test and compact letter display
M_chao_tukey <- TukeyHSD(M_chao)
cld_chao <- multcompLetters4(M_chao, M_chao_tukey)

# Table with the mean per site and the significance letters
dt_chao <- group_by(alpha_div, SiteID, Land_use) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(Chao1), sd = sd(Chao1), .groups = "drop")
dt_chao$cld <- cld_chao$SiteID$Letters[as.character(dt_chao$SiteID)]
```

```{r}
ggplot(alpha_div, aes(x = SiteID, y = Chao1)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = "mean", aes(fill = Land_use)) +
  geom_errorbar(data = dt_chao, aes(y = mean, ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd),
                width = 0.2) +
  geom_jitter(size = 2, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.1) +
  geom_text(data = dt_chao, aes(label = cld, y = max(alpha_div$Chao1) * 1.08)) +
  ylab("Estimated bacterial richness (Chao1)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

### Shannon diversity

```{r}
# ANOVA
M_shan <- aov(Shannon_div ~ SiteID, data = alpha_div)
anova(M_shan)

# Check the assumptions
shapiro.test(residuals(M_shan))
bartlett.test(Shannon_div ~ SiteID, data = alpha_div)

# Tukey test and compact letter display
M_shan_tukey <- TukeyHSD(M_shan)
cld_shan <- multcompLetters4(M_shan, M_shan_tukey)

# Table with the mean per site and the significance letters
dt_shan <- group_by(alpha_div, SiteID, Land_use) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(Shannon_div), sd = sd(Shannon_div), .groups = "drop")
dt_shan$cld <- cld_shan$SiteID$Letters[as.character(dt_shan$SiteID)]
```

```{r}
ggplot(alpha_div, aes(x = SiteID, y = Shannon_div)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = "mean", aes(fill = Land_use)) +
  geom_errorbar(data = dt_shan, aes(y = mean, ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd),
                width = 0.2) +
  geom_jitter(size = 2, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.1) +
  geom_text(data = dt_shan, aes(label = cld, y = max(alpha_div$Shannon_div) * 1.08)) +
  ylab("Bacterial Shannon diversity (q = 1)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

### Simpson diversity

```{r}
# ANOVA
M_simp <- aov(InvSimpson ~ SiteID, data = alpha_div)
anova(M_simp)

# Check the assumptions
shapiro.test(residuals(M_simp))
bartlett.test(InvSimpson ~ SiteID, data = alpha_div)

# Tukey test and compact letter display
M_simp_tukey <- TukeyHSD(M_simp)
cld_simp <- multcompLetters4(M_simp, M_simp_tukey)

# Table with the mean per site and the significance letters
dt_simp <- group_by(alpha_div, SiteID, Land_use) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(InvSimpson), sd = sd(InvSimpson), .groups = "drop")
dt_simp$cld <- cld_simp$SiteID$Letters[as.character(dt_simp$SiteID)]
```

```{r}
ggplot(alpha_div, aes(x = SiteID, y = InvSimpson)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = "mean", aes(fill = Land_use)) +
  geom_errorbar(data = dt_simp, aes(y = mean, ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd),
                width = 0.2) +
  geom_jitter(size = 2, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.1) +
  geom_text(data = dt_simp, aes(label = cld, y = max(alpha_div$InvSimpson) * 1.08)) +
  ylab("Bacterial Simpson diversity (q = 2)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

### Comparing measures

Compare the patterns of the four measures: richness gives the same weight to all OTUs, whereas Shannon and Simpson diversity give more weight to the abundant OTUs. If a site has a high richness but a low Simpson diversity, its community contains many rare OTUs but is dominated by a few abundant ones.
